To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the toxicity of a fragment of the prion protein, which reproduces the neuropathological changes occurring in the brains of patients with prion diseases, is accompanied by an increase in the levels of a gene encoding an enzyme involved in the detoxication of reactive oxygen species.
the toxicity of Prion Protein Fragment 1–106 (PrP) 106–126 in cultured neurons and astroglial cells is differentially associated with the induction of the heme oxygenase‐1 (HO‐1) mRNA.

PrP 106‐126, an amyloidogenic peptide corresponding to a fragment of the prion protein, induces heme oxygenase (a marker of oxidative stress) in cultured astrocytes, but not in cultured neurons, suggesting that the resistance of astrocyte to PrP 126 toxicity might be related to the ability of astrocytes to counteract oxidative stress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possible role of HO‐1 in PREs.
the induction of HO‐I mRNA in cultured neurons and astrocytes exposed to a PrP fragment.
the role of heme oxygenase‐1 in the pathophysiology of prion‐related disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HO‐1 induction in astroglial but not in neuronal cultures is a specific feature of PrP 107–126 toxicity.
the induction of HO‐ 1 mRNA by the peptide 106–126 in astroglial but not in neuronal cells might be an important mechanism in the resistance of astroglial cells to PrP 126 toxicity.
the PrP 106-126 peptide is not able to induce HO‐1 mRNA expression in cultured neurons, but it can induce HO-1 mRNA expression in astroglial cell culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amyloidogenic peptide PrP 106‐126 induces oxidative stress in astrocytes, and this is associated with an increase of HO‐1.
PrP 106-126 toxicity is mediated by oxidative stress and that the astroglial cell is a major target in prion diseases.
PrP 106-126 is a pro-oxidant peptide that induces oxidative stress in cultured astrocytes but not neurons, and that HO-1 induction is a response to this oxidative stress in astroglial cultures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PrP 106-126 induces heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) mRNA in astroglia but not in neurons.
PrP 106‐126, the most amyloidogenic fragment of PrP, is toxic to astrocytes, inducing HO‐1 mRNA.
the PrP 106-126 fragment induces HO-1 mRNA in rat astroglia cultures, but not in neurons, and the effect depends on the exposure time, concentration, and oxidative stress.
